newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook - Coffee may stay clear of $1,600.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook - Coffee may stay clear of $1,600.

text.p: Coffee futures will probably continue to scour the $1,615-$1,700 zone this week with good roaster interest protecting prices from a dip to $1,600, traders said on Monday.
Charts signalled a retreat to $1,600 earlier last week but Friday's strong close at $1,663 per tonne gave the market a technical facelift.

Elsewhere in soft commodities, cocoa will oscillate between strong technicals suggesting a fresh spike to 1,048 stg basis May and a clouded fundamental picture, while white sugar may be stuck in tight ranges.
Coffee brushed aside news last week that leading producers would release 500,000 60-kg bags of arabica coffee back to the market to ease supplies.

"It's half a million bags, which is not a slouch, but not a huge amount," said one trader. "Also, it's not certain that it's going to be ratified, for the simple reason that when they called this meeting coffee was at about 200 (cents/lb), now it's down to 170," he said.

The relaxation of export curbs was recommended by a technical group of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) and needs to be approved at a council in May, but some traders doubted this would happen.
"There is no reason for them to release more coffee now," said one. Others said additional coffee had probably been already sold and that Thursday's decision makes it formal.

Although traders could not rule out a descent to $1,600 on May, most were confident roaster buying would prop it up. But origins were ready to dump their stock each time the market hiked above $1,700, they said.

"I'm not convinced that it's going to do that (slip to $1,600). I think if it does, it's going to have a very long, hard battle. It's going to take most of the week to get down there," commented one trader.
Chart analysts said a break of $1,600 could send the May robusta down to the February low of $1,460.
The focus may shift to a possible transport workers' strike in Colombia next month but the market was unlikely to panic before this happens.
The arabica-robusta arbitrage could come in further from the present 93 cents on May as New York gradually loses ground amid a recovery in stocks.
Cocoa risked a loss of upside momentum after last week's failure to conquer the 1,035-40 stg resistance and with chart indicators still pointing to a correction.
"We have no fundamental data to push the market higher at the moment, unfortunately," said one trader.

May needs to clear initial resistance to make further headway towards the contract high of 1,075, but the uptrend remains intact while the contract stays above a crucial gap extending from 982, analyts said.

Traders will monitor the weather in Ivory Coast where crop experts expect the midcrop to reach above 100,000 tonnes and possibly even 160,000. The midcrop is the market's last hope for a supply squeeze after another huge Ivorian main crop this year.

In white sugar, New York should provide the key to London activity as both markets have been rangebound for some time, traders said. The whites were unlikely to break the recent range before the raws set the pace. London's spot May contract has meandered between $303.50 and $310.00 since the middle of last month.
"The London market is stuck...nobody is interested in getting involved until it (New York) breaks in a particular direction," said one trader.
"They don't want to go longer or shorter until they're forced to, either to take a profit or a loss."
More interest is being reported in the August/July differential but the majority of premium trades are currently confined to May/May, with sellers waiting in the wings at $69 and above.
Physical activity is expected to be muted with the approach of European Easter holiday break although Libya has postponed its recent whites buying tender to Monday.
London markets will be closed for Easter holiday on Friday and the following Monday.
